solution: Let \(u=\sqrt{x^2+16}\) and \(v=\dfrac{x}{x-1}\). Then \(\dfrac{du}{dx}=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+16}}\) and \(\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{-1}{(x-1)^2}\), so \(\dfrac{du}{dv}=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+16}}\cdot\big(-(x-1)^2\big)\). At \(x=5\): \(=\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{41}}\cdot(-16)=-\dfrac{80}{\sqrt{41}}\). Matches option A.

text: The derivative of \(f(\sec x)\) with respect to \(g(\tan x)\) at \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\), where \(f'(\sqrt{2})=4\) and \(g'(1)=2\), is
solution: \(\dfrac{d[f(\sec x)]}{d[g(\tan x)]}=\dfrac{f'(\sec x)\,\sec x\tan x}{g'(\tan x)\,\sec^2 x}=\dfrac{f'(\sec x)\tan x}{g'(\tan x)\sec x}\). At \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\sec x=\sqrt{2}\) and \(\tan x=1\): \(=\dfrac{f'(\sqrt{2})}{g'(1)\cdot\sqrt{2}}=\dfrac{4}{2\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}\). Matches option C.

text: The derivative of \(f(\tan x)\) w.r.t. \(g(\sec x)\) at \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\), where \(f'(1)=2\) and \(g'(\sqrt{2})=4\), is
solution: \(\dfrac{d[f(\tan x)]}{d[g(\sec x)]}=\dfrac{f'(\tan x)\,\sec^2 x}{g'(\sec x)\,\sec x\tan x}\). At \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\): numerator \(=f'(1)\cdot 2=4\); denominator \(=g'(\sqrt{2})\cdot\sqrt{2}=4\sqrt{2}\). So \(=\dfrac{4}{4\sqrt{2}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Matches option A.

Substitute \(t=\tan^{-1}x\), so \(dt=\dfrac{dx}{1+x^2}\). For \(x>0\), \(\sec^{-1}\sqrt{1+x^2}=t\) and \(\cos^{-1}\dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}=2t\), so the bracket \(=t^2+2t\). Then \(\int e^t(t^2+2t)\,dt=\int e^t\big(f+f'\big)\,dt\) with \(f=t^2\), giving \(e^t t^2+c=\left(\tan^{-1}x\right)^2 e^{\tan^{-1}x}+c\). Matches option A. (The source 2024 paper prints options (c) and (d) identically — a printed-paper defect; both are non-answers.
